Threshold · Lecture 1 · The blue, stations 1–2

The blue

One jar's blue, followed through all four.

A jar painted in blue under its glaze: potters at Jingdezhen made it in the 1300s, and the record does not give their names. A network is four flows at once, objects, materials, skills and people; they share routes, but not terms.

claimsf13-e-jarF1.13-C01F1.13-C02sourcesF1.13-C01F1.13-C02
captionL1 · 1

On the stage, the jar with blue underglaze decoration that the Cleveland Museum of Art holds as 1962.154: Jingdezhen, the 1300s, made by potters and painters whose names the record does not give. The map settles on Jingdezhen; the jar's century sits as a bar on the objects lane.

prompt · L1.predict-1L1 · 1

The jar's blue, Jingdezhen, the 1300s: where did the blue come from, Jingdezhen's own hills, Iran, or Europe?

  • Jingdezhen's own hills
  • Iran
  • Europe
saydrawn after the guess

Cleveland's record says the cobalt was imported from Iran, likely from Kashan. The dashed leg from Kashan to Jingdezhen is drawn after the guess; it marks a material, not an object.

answeron the map: the leg r01 Kashan → Jingdezhen, Kashan lit; never a beatclaimsf13-e-jarF1.13-C02
focus · mark f13-e-xuandeL1 · 1

Jingdezhen, 1426–1435: Jiang and colleagues tested imperial wares of the Xuande reign and write that early blue-and-white relied heavily on imported cobalt from the West. The bar on the materials lane is their sample.

claimsf13-e-xuandeF1.13-C03sourcesF1.13-C03
captionL1 · 2

On the stage, a footed bowl from Iran with a blue rim, fritware, pierced and painted under the glaze: the Cleveland Museum of Art dates it late 1100s–early 1200s and holds it as 1915.581. Blue under a glaze was in Kashan's workshops a century before the Jingdezhen jar; the map tightens on Kashan.

claimsf13-e-kashan-bowlF1.13-C05F1.13-C02sourcesF1.13-C05F1.13-C02
note · argued · a-cobalt-mineL1 · 2

Which mine gave the cobalt in Kashan's blue is argued; the lecture does not choose. One reading: Qamsar, near Kashan, where Abu'l-Qasim's treatise of 1301 places lâjvard, the blue, the most cited source. The other: deposits near Anarak, 200 kilometres east of Kashan, which Jiang and colleagues propose in their discussion. The two fuzzy marks on the map are the two readings; Cleveland places the bowl probably at Kashan.

bridge · the map scale changesL1 · 7

Kashan → Amsterdam · Iran at zoom 5.5 → Asia at zoom 1.95

From Kashan and the cobalt of the 1300s to Amsterdam and a Kraak dish of about 1600–1625: the blue that came from Iran leaves China as export ware. The map opens from Iran to the whole of Asia for station 7, The blue goes north.
